dough-water-temperature.formula: factor_count = preferment_temp_f > 0 ? 4 : 3; water_temp_f = desired_dough_temp_f x factor_count - (flour_temp_f + room_temp_f + friction_factor_f + (preferment used ? preferment_temp_f : 0)).
dough-water-temperature.edition: Desired dough temperature (DDT) mixing-water calculation (Hamelman, Bread; Bread Bakers Guild of America / San Francisco Baking Institute), by name; the measured friction factor for the specific mixer and batch and the baker's finished-dough temperature reading govern.
dough-water-temperature.freeAccess: The DDT method is public baking practice; the desired dough temperature, flour and room temperatures, and the mixer's friction factor are the bakery's measured values.
dough-water-temperature.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dough-water-temperature.editionNote: Because the speed of fermentation depends strongly on dough temperature, a baker aims for a specific desired dough temperature, or DDT, and hits it by adjusting the one input under real-time control: the mixing water. The method treats the finished dough temperature as the average of a set of temperature 'factors,' so the total of all factors is the DDT times how many there are. Solving for the water gives the DDT times the number of factors, minus every other factor's temperature. A straight dough has three factors -- the flour, the room (which stands in for the ambient and the ingredients equilibrated to it), and the friction of mixing -- so the water temperature is the DDT times three, less the flour, room, and friction temperatures. When a preferment such as a poolish, biga, or levain is added, it becomes a fourth factor and the multiplier becomes four, subtracting the preferment temperature as well. The friction factor is the temperature rise the mechanical action of mixing adds to the dough; it is a property of the specific mixer and batch size, determined once by comparing a measured finished dough temperature against the prediction, and it runs roughly 0 to 5 degrees Fahrenheit for hand mixing and about 24 to 30 for a spiral mixer at speed. To reach a 75-degree DDT with 68-degree flour, a 72-degree room, and a 24-degree friction factor, the water must be 75 times 3 minus the sum 164, or 61 degrees; with a 74-degree preferment and a 78-degree DDT at a 26-degree friction factor, the water is 78 times 4 minus 235, or 77 degrees. If the required water comes out below freezing, part of the water is weighed out and added as ice; if it comes out implausibly hot, the friction factor is almost certainly mis-estimated. This is a working setpoint; the actual measured friction factor for the specific mixer and batch, and the baker's own finished-dough temperature reading, govern.

assumptions.name: DDT water calculation
assumptions.value: water = DDT x N - (other factors + friction); N = 3 (flour, room, friction) or 4 (adds a preferment)

assumptions.name: Friction factor
assumptions.value: the mixer's temperature rise, measured per mixer/batch: ~0-5 F hand, ~24-30 F spiral; below freezing, add weighed ice

dressing-percentage.formula: dressing_pct = 100 x hot_carcass_weight_lb / live_weight_lb; chilled_carcass_lb = hot_carcass_weight_lb x (1 - chill_shrink_pct / 100); boneless_yield_lb = chilled_carcass_lb x cutting_yield_pct / 100.
dressing-percentage.edition: Carcass dressing percentage and cutting yield (standard meat-science figures: beef ~60-64%, pork ~72-75%, lamb ~50%; beef cutting yield ~65-70% of the carcass), by name; the processor's certified scale and the cut sheet govern the actual freezer yield.
dressing-percentage.freeAccess: The dressing-percentage ratio and cutting-yield fractions are public meat-science practice; the live weight, carcass weight, and cutting yield are the animal's and processor's values.
dressing-percentage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dressing-percentage.editionNote: Dressing percentage measures how much of a live slaughter animal ends up as carcass, and it is the starting point for pricing freezer beef, pork, or lamb. It is the hot carcass weight -- the weight of the carcass immediately after slaughter, before it chills, with the head, hide, feet, and internal organs removed -- divided by the animal's live weight. A 1,200-pound steer that yields a 744-pound carcass dresses at 744 divided by 1,200, or 62.0%, which is typical for beef at roughly 60 to 64%. Pork dresses higher, around 72 to 75%, because the skin and feet remain on the carcass: a 260-pound market hog with a 190-pound carcass dresses at 73.1%. Lamb dresses lower, near 50%. What actually fills the freezer, though, is much less than the carcass weight, because the carcass still contains bone, trim fat, and unavoidable cutting loss. The carcass also loses about 3.5 to 4% of its weight as moisture in the cooler, and the cutting yield of about 65 to 70% applies to that chilled carcass, so the 744-pound carcass chills to about 718 pounds and produces 718 times 0.67, or about 481 pounds, of cut-and-wrapped meat (UW-Madison Extension's worked example). Dressing percentage rises with fatter, more heavily muscled, and lighter-gutted animals, and falls with gut fill from a full rumen and with a heavy or muddy hide. This is a pricing and planning aid; the actual live and carcass weights come from the processor's certified scale, and the specific cut sheet chosen, the dry-aging shrink, and the packer or custom locker govern the final freezer yield.

assumptions.name: Dressing and cutting yield
assumptions.value: dressing % = hot carcass / live x 100; chilled = hot x (1 - shrink), shrink about 3.5-4%; take-home = chilled carcass x cutting yield; beef 60-64%, pork 72-75%, lamb ~50% dressing; beef cutting yield ~65-70%

assumptions.name: Freezer yield
assumptions.value: boneless take-home is well below the carcass (bone, trim, cutting loss); the processor's scale, cut sheet, and aging shrink govern

manure-application-rate.formula: available_per_unit = total_nutr x availability/100; rate = crop_need / available_per_unit; applied = rate x available_per_unit = crop_need.
manure-application-rate.edition: The nutrient-based manure application rate per USDA NRCS Conservation Practice Standard 590 (Nutrient Management), by name.
manure-application-rate.freeAccess: NRCS Code 590 and manure-management guidance are free at nrcs.usda.gov and from land-grant extension. A manure test and the farm's nutrient-management plan govern.
manure-application-rate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
manure-application-rate.editionNote: The available nutrient per unit = total nutrient x first-year availability fraction, and the application rate = crop nutrient requirement / available per unit (ton/acre for solid manure, 1,000 gal/acre for liquid). The rate is set by the most limiting of nitrogen or P2O5 under the farm's nutrient-management plan. This returns the single-nutrient rate for the entered availability: it takes the plant-available fraction as entered (not by a mineralization model), does not run a phosphorus-index or the P-based cap that often governs, and is not itself a nutrient-management plan. NRCS Code 590 and the farm's certified plan govern.

assumptions.name: Nutrient-based rate
assumptions.value: rate = crop_need / (total_nutr x availability); closes to applied = crop_need

assumptions.name: Form units
assumptions.value: ton/acre for solid manure (lb/ton), 1,000 gal/acre for liquid (lb/1,000 gal)

assumptions.name: Limiting nutrient
assumptions.value: the plan sets whether N or P2O5 governs; a P-index can force a lower rate

drainage-invert.formula: Total fall = slope x run; invert-out = invert-in - fall; top of pipe = invert-out + OD; cover = surface - top of pipe. Slope entered as in/ft or percent, normalized to ft/ft.
drainage-invert.edition: IPC 2021 (International Plumbing Code). Section 704 (drainage piping slope minimums).
drainage-invert.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
drainage-invert.editionNote: Editions available: bundled values follow IPC 2021. Jurisdictions on IPC 2018 / 2024 differ in fixture-unit values and vent-sizing tables; verify the edition adopted by your AHJ. UPC-jurisdictions (CA, IN, MA, NV, parts of NJ) use the Uniform Plumbing Code instead. The minimum-cover and maximum-depth limits, the local frost depth, and the live-load bury requirement are set by the adopted code and the engineer/survey of record; the minimum cover compared against is the user-supplied governing value.

assumptions.name: Cover datum
assumptions.value: cover measured from finished grade to the top of the pipe (invert-out + OD / 12)

assumptions.name: Sign convention
assumptions.value: a negative cover (pipe crown above grade) is flagged, not rejected

cistern-storage-days.formula: reserve_days = usable_storage_gal / daily_demand_gpd; required_gal_for_target = daily_demand_gpd x target_days.
cistern-storage-days.edition: Rainwater-harvesting / off-grid storage mass balance (ARCSA / TWDB rainwater manuals; water-storage practice), by name; local rainfall or the source yield and the AHJ govern.
cistern-storage-days.freeAccess: The reserve relations are a public first-principles mass balance (storage over demand; demand times days); the usable storage, demand, and target come from the tank detail and the water budget.
cistern-storage-days.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
cistern-storage-days.editionNote: A straight storage mass balance. The reserve a tank carries is its usable storage divided by the daily demand, and the tank needed to bank a target dry spell is the daily demand times the target days. USABLE storage is what sits above the pump-intake dead volume and below the overflow, past any reserved fire-suppression or first-flush volume. Use a realistic PEAK daily demand (not the annual average), because the reserve has to survive the worst stretch. For a rain-fed cistern the reserve must bridge the longest dry spell between meaningful rains, sized off the local rainfall record; for a hauled or well-fed tank it sets the refill interval. This is a planning estimate; the local rainfall or the source yield, the storage tank detail, and the AHJ (for a potable system) govern.

assumptions.name: Usable storage
assumptions.value: above the pump-intake dead volume and below overflow, past any fire / first-flush reserve

assumptions.name: Peak demand
assumptions.value: use a realistic peak daily demand, not the annual average; the reserve must bridge the worst stretch

tanker-shuttle-cycle.formula: fill_min = tank_gal / fill_gpm; dump_min = tank_gal / dump_gpm; travel_min = 2 x distance_mi / speed_mph x 60; cycle_min = fill_min + dump_min + travel_min; single_tanker_gpm = tank_gal / cycle_min.
tanker-shuttle-cycle.edition: IFSTA / NFPA 1142 rural water-supply shuttle cycle time, by name.
tanker-shuttle-cycle.freeAccess: The shuttle cycle-time relation is public fire-service / rural water-supply training material; incident command governs the actual operation.
tanker-shuttle-cycle.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
tanker-shuttle-cycle.editionNote: The travel is the round trip (both directions) - counting only one way understates the cycle and oversizes the flow. The tank load is the usable water actually moved (ISO credits about 90% of nominal - use that here); the fill and dump rates are the site-limited rates, not the pump nameplate. A single tanker sustains only tank / cycle, so rural supply needs a fleet - feed this cycle to tanker-shuttle-flow for the fleet flow. The fill-site capacity and the operation govern - a planning aid, not incident command.

assumptions.name: Round-trip travel
assumptions.value: travel time counts both directions (2 x one-way); the tank load is the usable ~90% of nominal

assumptions.name: Site-limited rates
assumptions.value: fill and dump are the site-limited rates, not the pump nameplate; the slow site dominates the cycle

search-track-spacing.formula: coverage = sweep_width / track_spacing; POD = 1 - e^(-coverage); track_spacing = sweep_width / (-ln(1 - target_POD)).
search-track-spacing.edition: NSARC / USCG search theory (exponential random-search detection model), by name.
search-track-spacing.freeAccess: Search-theory relations are public (US Coast Guard / NSARC references); the incident commander and search plan govern.
search-track-spacing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.
search-track-spacing.editionNote: The sweep width must first be corrected for weather, fatigue, terrain, and speed (the raw detection range overstates it); the exponential random-search model is conservative and parallel-track sweeps reach a higher POD at the same coverage; this is single-pass POD (multiple passes compound via search-probability). A planning aid, not a guarantee of detection.

assumptions.name: Detection model
assumptions.value: exponential (random-search) POD = 1 - e^(-coverage); conservative vs parallel-track

tip-out.formula: Each member's share = (member hours / total hours) x total amount.
tip-out.freeAccess: No licensed source required. The split is definitional arithmetic; the pool, the roles, and the point weights come from house policy and from the wage-and-hour rules that govern tip pooling.
tip-out.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.

accessible-shower-check.formula: transfer type: 36 x 36 in clear inside, 36 in wide entry, 36 x 48 in clearance from the control wall. Standard roll-in: 30 in wide by 60 in deep clear inside, 60 in wide entry, 30 x 60 in clearance adjacent to the open face. Alternate roll-in: 36 in wide by 60 in deep clear inside, 36 in wide entry at one end of the long side.
accessible-shower-check.edition: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, 608.2.1, 608.2.2, and 608.2.3. A US federal standard in the public domain, quoted directly.
accessible-shower-check.freeAccess: The 2010 ADA Standards are published in full at no cost at ada.gov and by the US Access Board.
accessible-shower-check.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
accessible-shower-check.editionNote: Three types with three different geometries, and picking the wrong one is what puts a bathroom remodel a foot short in the wrong direction. The TRANSFER type is the small one - 36 in square, the only one of the three that fits a standard 36 in alcove where a tub used to be - and what surprises people is its OUTSIDE clearance: 36 in wide by 48 in long measured from the CONTROL WALL, deeper than the stall itself. The fixture is small and the room it needs is not, which is the reverse of how a plan reads. The STANDARD ROLL-IN is 30 in wide by 60 in deep, and its entry is the WHOLE LONG SIDE at 60 in wide minimum - so a 30 in stall that reads as tight on a plan is correct, and what defeats it is anything built across the opening: a curb, a jamb, a door, a fixed panel. The ALTERNATE ROLL-IN trades entry width for stall width, 36 by 60 in inside with a 36 in wide entry at one end of the long side, and it is the type that fits where a 60 in tub was and a full-width opening is impossible. Because the three overlap in confusing ways, the tile also reports which types a compartment as built WOULD satisfy, in either orientation - worth knowing before anything is torn out, since a stall that fails the type it was drawn as often meets another. Not checked: grab bars, which differ by type and are the reason the three are not interchangeable; the seat, which a transfer shower requires and a standard roll-in requires only in some configurations; controls, faucets, and the hand shower, whose location is tied to the seat and the entry; thresholds and the limit on a roll-in curb; the shower spray unit and hose; enclosures, which may not obstruct transfer or the clear floor space; drainage and slope; and state and local accessibility law and the plumbing code. A compartment sizing screen, not a bathroom design.

assumptions.name: Transfer type
assumptions.value: 36 x 36 in inside, 36 in entry, 36 x 48 in clearance from the control wall

assumptions.name: Standard roll-in
assumptions.value: 30 x 60 in inside, 60 in entry, 30 x 60 in clearance at the open face

assumptions.name: Alternate roll-in
assumptions.value: 36 x 60 in inside, 36 in entry at one end of the long side

assumptions.name: Inside dimensions
assumptions.value: measured at the center points of opposing sides

assumptions.name: What it would satisfy
assumptions.value: reported in either orientation, as information rather than a verdict

molarity-dilution.formula: C1 * V1 = C2 * V2. Solve for the missing fourth.
molarity-dilution.governance: Verify protocol against your lab's SOP before pipetting. A miscalculated dilution can ruin a run or a sample.

assumptions.name: Conservation
assumptions.value: moles before = moles after; total mass / volume conserved

sales-tax-nexus.formula: Lookup by state into a per-state row with sales threshold (USD), optional transactions threshold, citation, and verified-on date.
sales-tax-nexus.edition: Per-state department of revenue published nexus guidance, post-Wayfair (South Dakota v. Wayfair, Inc., 138 S. Ct. 2080 (2018)).
sales-tax-nexus.freeAccess: Each state's DOR site publishes its current nexus rule.
sales-tax-nexus.governance: This is legal information, not legal advice. Statutes and court rules change. Verify with current state code and a licensed attorney before relying on this for a filing or a deadline.
sales-tax-nexus.editionNote: Quarterly cadence per spec-v5.md 8 recheck schedule.

assumptions.name: Threshold lookback
assumptions.value: prior or current calendar year (most states)

assumptions.name: Sales tax vs. use tax
assumptions.value: thresholds shown trigger collection / remittance obligation; consumer-side use-tax is separate

osha-recordkeeping.formula: Reference page; no compute. Each entry is a (topic, note) record authored by the project.
osha-recordkeeping.edition: 29 CFR 1904 by section number only. Original plain-English summary.
osha-recordkeeping.governance: Math aid for personal verification. Stop work and consult the qualified person on site if any number does not match the field condition.
osha-recordkeeping.editionNote: Annual cadence: review when OSHA publishes a Federal Register update.

assumptions.name: Industry exemptions
assumptions.value: low-hazard industries listed in 29 CFR 1904.2 are partially exempt; user verifies their NAICS classification

mixed-water-temp.formula: T_blend = (Qh*Th + Qc*Tc)/(Qh+Qc); inverse hot fraction = (T_target - Tc)/(Th - Tc); hot:cold ratio = (T_target - Tc)/(Th - T_target).
mixed-water-temp.edition: First-principles mixing energy balance for blending hot and cold potable water; the delivery-temperature limits follow the ASSE 1017 (master tempering) and ASSE 1016/1070 (point-of-use scald-guard) device standards and the IPC/UPC scald provisions, by name.
mixed-water-temp.freeAccess: Public first-principles energy balance. The listed mixing valve and the AHJ govern the installed setpoint.
mixed-water-temp.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
mixed-water-temp.editionNote: Single-edition (first-principles mixing). Scald limits: <= 120 F for shower, tub-shower and tub-filler valves (IPC 424.3 / 424.5), <= 110 F at public hand-washing fixtures (IPC 416.5, ASSE 1070).

assumptions.name: Same fluid
assumptions.value: hot and cold are the same fluid (water); the balance is by flow-weighted temperature

pipe-velocity.formula: Continuity: v (ft/s) = 0.4085 * gpm / d^2 (d = actual inside diameter, in); inverse gpm = v * d^2 / 0.4085.
pipe-velocity.edition: Pipe-flow velocity from continuity (v = 0.4085*gpm/d^2) and the copper erosion-corrosion velocity limits (about 5 ft/s hot, 8 ft/s cold) per the Copper Development Association / ASTM and ASPE plumbing-design guidance, by name; first-principles.
pipe-velocity.freeAccess: Public first-principles continuity. Actual inside diameter (not nominal) governs; the material erosion-corrosion ceiling is the design limit.
pipe-velocity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed plumber / gas fitter govern. Verify against the IPC / IFGC edition adopted in your jurisdiction.
pipe-velocity.editionNote: Single-edition (continuity). Copper ceiling about 5 ft/s hot, 8 ft/s cold; the hot/cold service is a labeled toggle. Pairs with pipe-sizing and friction-loss.

assumptions.name: Inside diameter
assumptions.value: the actual bore for the material/size, not the nominal size

smoke-detector-spacing-count.formula: detectors = rows x cols, the fewest grid cells that each fit the listed S x S square or keep every point within 0.7 S (NFPA 72 17.7.4.2.3.1); wall_max_ft = listed_spacing_ft / 2.
smoke-detector-spacing-count.edition: NFPA 72 spot-detector grid identity by name (grid count over the listed spacing; wall maximum at half the spacing); first-principles grid arithmetic.
smoke-detector-spacing-count.freeAccess: The grid arithmetic is public first-principles; the listed spacing comes from the device listing and the reductions from NFPA 72.
smoke-detector-spacing-count.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
smoke-detector-spacing-count.editionNote: The listed spacing (about 30 ft for spot smoke on a smooth ceiling) comes from the device listing. The 0.7-times-spacing rule confirms no point is farther than that from a detector; the first detector sits within half the spacing of each wall. Beams, high ceilings, and HVAC reduce the spacing per NFPA 72. Like sprinkler-head-layout, this is an install estimate the stamped fire-alarm plan and the AHJ plan-review govern.

assumptions.name: Listed spacing
assumptions.value: ~30 ft for spot smoke on a smooth ceiling; the device listing governs

assumptions.name: Coverage
assumptions.value: 0.7 x spacing to the farthest point; first detector within spacing/2 of each wall

drypipe-air-compressor.formula: system_ft3 = dry_volume_gal / 7.48; free_air_cfm = system_ft3 x (normal_pressure_psig / 14.7) / restore_minutes.
drypipe-air-compressor.edition: NFPA 13 (Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems) dry-pipe / preaction air-restoration time limit (about 30 minutes), by name; the compressor rating and the AHJ govern.
drypipe-air-compressor.freeAccess: The free-air relation is public first-principles (system volume x gauge-to-atmospheric ratio over the restore time); the system volume comes from the pipe schedule and the pressure and restore time from NFPA 13 and the AHJ.
drypipe-air-compressor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
drypipe-air-compressor.editionNote: The free-air CFM a compressor must deliver to restore a dry-pipe or double-interlock-preaction system's normal air pressure within the NFPA 13 time limit -- 30 minutes for a standard system (some are allowed 60). The free air needed to pressurize the system volume to its normal gauge pressure is the volume times the gauge-to-atmospheric ratio (P / 14.7), and dividing by the restore time gives the compressor's required free-air CFM; the next larger listed unit is selected. A dedicated, LISTED automatic air-maintenance device is required (not a portable shop compressor), and an air source that mitigates internal corrosion, or supervised nitrogen, is preferred. The system volume comes from the pipe schedule, the normal air pressure is set to hold the dry-pipe clapper closed with the required margin over the trip point, and NFPA 13 and the AHJ set the restore time. A sizing estimate; the compressor manufacturer's rating at the operating pressure governs the pick.

assumptions.name: Restore time
assumptions.value: NFPA 13: restore normal air pressure within ~30 min (60 min allowed for some systems)

assumptions.name: Listed device
assumptions.value: a listed automatic air-maintenance device is required, not a shop compressor; nitrogen mitigates corrosion

paraboloid-volume.formula: Full V = (1/2) pi R^2 H (half the enclosing cylinder); apex-up partial fill V(y) = pi R^2 y^2/(2H), with the wetted radius r(y) = R sqrt(y/H); percent full = (y/H)^2.
paraboloid-volume.edition: The paraboloid of revolution volume - standard solid geometry (Pappus's theorem / integration) as in Machinery's Handbook (Industrial Press), by name; public domain.
paraboloid-volume.freeAccess: Pure solid geometry, public; the base diameter, height, and fill depth are user-supplied.
paraboloid-volume.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
paraboloid-volume.editionNote: Volume of a paraboloid of revolution - the solid a plane parabolic segment cannot give: the full volume is V = (1/2) pi R^2 H, exactly half the cylinder of the same base radius R and height H that boxes it (between the cone's 1/3 and the cylinder's 1). Because a parabola runs the axial coordinate z in proportion to r^2, filling from the apex the wetted radius grows as r(y) = R sqrt(y/H) and the liquid volume as V(y) = pi R^2 y^2/(2H), so it fills as the SQUARE of the depth and a stick at half the height reads only a quarter full (percent = (y/H)^2). Use it for a spun-cast dish, a parabolic reflector blank, a dished or parabolic vessel bottom, or the free surface a spinning liquid takes. Reported in cubic feet and US gallons. A circular dish is the spherical-cap-volume tile; a cone is frustum-volume with a zero top; an off-axis or tilted paraboloid is separate. A shop and takeoff aid; verify critical dimensions on the work.

assumptions.name: Full volume
assumptions.value: V = (1/2) pi R^2 H, half the enclosing cylinder

assumptions.name: Partial fill
assumptions.value: V(y) = pi R^2 y^2/(2H) from the apex, r(y) = R sqrt(y/H); fills as the square of depth
assumptions.source: integration of the parabola z ~ r^2

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: solid of revolution about the axis; an off-axis or tilted paraboloid is separate

speed-of-sound-air.formula: c = 331.3 sqrt(1 + T_C/273.15) m/s (dry air, from c = sqrt(gamma R T / M)); ft/s = m/s x 3.28084; propagation delay = 1000 / c_ftps ms per foot. T_C = (T_F - 32)/1.8.
speed-of-sound-air.edition: First-principles kinetic theory (c = sqrt(gamma R T / M)) with the NIST/standard 331.3 m/s dry-air reference at 0 C, by name.
speed-of-sound-air.freeAccess: The speed-of-sound-vs-temperature relation is public first-principles physics; the 331.3 m/s reference at 0 C is a standard NIST value and the air temperature is the user's input.
speed-of-sound-air.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
speed-of-sound-air.editionNote: The speed of sound in dry air from the temperature, c = 331.3 sqrt(1 + T_C/273.15) m/s (equivalently sqrt(gamma R T / M) with gamma 1.4 and air's molar mass), converted to ft/s. It is the propagation speed the time-alignment and ceiling-speaker-coverage tiles assume as a fixed ~1130 ft/s, but it swings about 6% from a freezing morning to a hot afternoon: 1,087 ft/s at 32 F, 1,126 ft/s at 68 F (the usual 1,130 rule of thumb), 1,155 ft/s at 95 F. Because the delay required at a fixed distance is inversely proportional to c, re-timing an outdoor delay tower for the day's temperature keeps arrivals aligned; the propagation delay is 1000 / c ms per foot (about 0.888 ms/ft at 68 F). This is dry air; humidity raises c slightly (a small second-order term) and altitude alone does not change it (temperature does). A first-principles aid; the measured system tuning governs.

assumptions.name: Speed of sound
assumptions.value: c = 331.3 sqrt(1 + T_C/273.15) m/s (dry air), from c = sqrt(gamma R T / M)

assumptions.name: Propagation delay
assumptions.value: 1000 / c_ftps ms per foot; delay is inversely proportional to c

assumptions.name: Dry air
assumptions.value: humidity is a small second-order correction; altitude alone does not change c

true-airspeed.formula: sigma = (1 - 6.87535e-6 h)^4.2559 (h = density altitude in ft, troposphere); TAS = CAS / sqrt(sigma). Rule of thumb: TAS ~ CAS (1 + 0.02 h/1000).
true-airspeed.edition: True airspeed from calibrated airspeed and the ISA density ratio, per the FAA Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge and the ICAO Standard Atmosphere, by name; first-principles.
true-airspeed.freeAccess: The TAS = CAS/sqrt(sigma) relation and the ISA density-ratio formula are public FAA/ICAO standard-atmosphere physics; the CAS and density altitude are the user's inputs.
true-airspeed.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
true-airspeed.editionNote: The true airspeed from the calibrated airspeed and the density altitude, the conversion the density-altitude tile leads up to and the turn-radius-bank tile consumes. The airspeed indicator senses dynamic pressure (half rho V squared), so in thinner air the same indicated speed is a faster true speed: TAS = CAS / sqrt(sigma), sigma the density ratio rho/rho0. At the density altitude sigma = (1 - 6.87535e-6 h)^4.2559 with h in feet - 1.000 at sea level, 0.862 at 5,000 ft (TAS 7.7% over CAS), 0.739 at 10,000 ft (16.4% over). A 120 KCAS climb at 8,000 ft density altitude is 135 KTAS. The +2%/1000 ft rule of thumb reads a few knots HIGH (3.8 kt at 120 KCAS and 8,000 ft), with the gap peaking near 15,000 ft and closing by about 25,000 ft; above that it reads low. This treats CAS as equal to equivalent airspeed (the low-speed assumption; the compressibility correction to EAS matters only at high speed and altitude), and TAS is airspeed - add the wind vector for ground speed. A planning estimate; the aircraft flight manual and the pilot in command govern.

assumptions.name: TAS relation
assumptions.value: TAS = CAS / sqrt(sigma), sigma the ISA density ratio at the density altitude

assumptions.name: Density ratio
assumptions.value: sigma = (1 - 6.87535e-6 h)^4.2559, h in ft (troposphere, <= 36,089 ft)

assumptions.name: Low-speed
assumptions.value: CAS ~ EAS assumed; the compressibility correction matters only at high speed/altitude; TAS is not ground speed

machine-room-heat.formula: heat while running = input power x (1 - efficiency) x 3,412.142 BTU/h per kW; average = that x duty cycle; total = average + controller standby + lighting and envelope gains; tons = total / 12,000; temperature rise with no cooling = total / (0.018 x room volume).
machine-room-heat.edition: Loss-based heat rejection at the exact 3,412.142 BTU per hour per kilowatt, averaged over an entered peak-hour duty cycle, by name, with ASME A17.1 and the equipment manufacturer's environmental limits named. Manufacturer heat rejection data for the specific machine and drive is the authority.
machine-room-heat.freeAccess: Arithmetic on equipment data the user reads off the machine and drive; no manufacturer performance table is reproduced.
machine-room-heat.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
machine-room-heat.editionNote: The heat is the inefficiency, which makes it a smaller number than people expect but a persistent one, and because elevators run intermittently the average over a peak hour is what a cooling system has to remove. The consequence of exceeding the equipment's limit is specific and bad: modern drives monitor their own temperature and shut down to protect themselves, and an elevator that shuts down mid-trip is an entrapment requiring a rescue. That is why machine room cooling in most jurisdictions is a required system rather than a comfort provision, and why it is often required to be on standby power alongside the elevator itself. The sources beyond the machine are what get left out. A machine room on a roof with a west-facing wall and no insulation gains solar heat through the envelope that can exceed the equipment's own contribution; the controller draws standby power continuously even when the car is parked; and a room shared with other equipment inherits its heat too. A cooling load computed from the machine alone will be short, and one computed from the machine's connected power rather than its losses will be several times too large. The no-cooling temperature rise reported here assumes the room loses no heat at all through its envelope, so it is a fastest-case bound rather than a prediction.

assumptions.name: Heat is the loss, not the connected load
assumptions.value: using connected power overstates it several times over on an efficient machine

assumptions.name: The controller and the envelope are not optional terms
assumptions.value: standby power is continuous and a roof machine room can gain more than the equipment makes

assumptions.name: Over-temperature is an entrapment
assumptions.value: drives shut down to protect themselves, possibly with passengers aboard

panic-hardware-force.formula: each measured force is compared to its own entered limit; the actuating portion must be at least half the door leaf width; the bar must sit between 34 and 48 in above the floor.
panic-hardware-force.edition: The egress door operating force limits by name -- release of the latch, force to set the door in motion, and force to swing it to full open, each measured separately -- with the actuating portion and mounting height requirements named, and NFPA 80 cited for rated doors. Limits are entered from the adopted code.
panic-hardware-force.freeAccess: Comparison of the user's own gauge readings against limits they enter; no code table is reproduced.
panic-hardware-force.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
panic-hardware-force.editionNote: Three separate forces are measured and they fail for different reasons. Release force is the bar itself, and a high reading points at the device: binding, a bent bar, a latch dragging on a misaligned strike, or a device never lubricated. Set-in-motion and swing forces are the door, and a high reading there points at the closer, the hinges, or a pressure difference across the opening. That last cause is the one people miss: a stair door in a pressurized stairwell can be well within every hardware specification and still take far more than its limit to move, because the building is holding it shut, and the harder the stairwell is pressurized for smoke control the worse it gets. Release passing while set-in-motion fails is the signature of something holding the door shut rather than something wrong with the bar, and replacing the exit device would change nothing. Fire exit hardware carries an additional constraint that gets violated with good intentions: on a rated door the latch must engage, so a device dogged down to make a door swing freely for convenience has defeated a fire door, and only listed fire exit hardware without a dogging feature belongs on a rated opening.

assumptions.name: Three forces, three different causes
assumptions.value: release points at the device; set-in-motion and swing point at the door and its environment

assumptions.name: Pressurization can fail a compliant door
assumptions.value: the building holds it shut, and adjusting the closer trades a reading for latching

assumptions.name: Dogging a rated door defeats it
assumptions.value: only listed fire exit hardware without a dogging feature belongs on a rated opening

blast-scaled-distance-ppv.formula: scaled distance = distance / sqrt(charge weight per delay); PPV = K x scaled distance raised to minus b; the largest charge at a required scaled distance = (distance / required SD) squared; the compliant distance = sqrt(charge) x (K / limit) raised to one over b.
blast-scaled-distance-ppv.edition: The square-root scaled distance and the site propagation relation by name, with the regulatory minimum-scaled-distance compliance path named as an alternative to seismograph monitoring. Site constants are entered; a site-specific regression from seismograph records is the defensible basis. Blasting is a licensed activity: the blaster in charge, the state and federal explosives regulations, MSHA or OSHA jurisdiction, and the site's blast plan govern.
blast-scaled-distance-ppv.freeAccess: Power-law arithmetic on constants and limits the user supplies; no regulatory table is reproduced.
blast-scaled-distance-ppv.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
blast-scaled-distance-ppv.editionNote: Vibration scales with charge weight per DELAY, not per shot, which is the whole reason delay initiation exists. A large shot fired on many delays produces the vibration of one delay's charge, and that single fact is what lets a quarry work near a town at all; reading the charge weight per shot into this relation overstates the vibration enormously and is its most common misuse. The propagation constants are site-specific and vary widely with geology. Generic values can be wrong by a factor of two in either direction, and a site-specific regression from actual seismograph records is what a serious operation uses. That is why most regulations offer two compliance paths: monitor every shot with a seismograph, or stay above a prescribed minimum scaled distance and skip the monitoring, the second being conservative by design. What this does not evaluate is FREQUENCY, and every modern vibration limit is frequency-dependent: the same peak particle velocity is acceptable at 40 Hz and not at 6 Hz, because low frequencies couple into structures. It does not address airblast or flyrock, and it does not perform a preblast survey, which is what actually resolves damage claims.

assumptions.name: Per delay, never per shot
assumptions.value: delay initiation is what makes the arithmetic work, and the misuse overstates vibration enormously

assumptions.name: Generic constants can be wrong by a factor of two
assumptions.value: a site-specific seismograph regression is the defensible basis

assumptions.name: Limits are frequency-dependent
assumptions.value: and this evaluates no frequency at all

dryer-duct-length.formula: fitting equivalent = (90-elbow count x equivalent length per 90) + (45-elbow count x equivalent length per 45); developed length = straight run + fitting equivalent; compliant when developed length <= the maximum allowable length; remaining straight run = max - developed; label required when developed length exceeds 35 ft.
dryer-duct-length.edition: IRC M1502.4.6 (maximum exhaust duct length measured from the connection to the transition duct to the outlet terminal, reduced by fitting equivalent lengths, and not including the transition duct); M1502.4.6.2 (the dryer manufacturer's installation instructions determine the size and maximum length, with the code's fitting table used only in the absence of manufacturer equivalent lengths); M1502.4.7 (equivalent length identified on a permanent label or tag within 6 ft of the duct connection where it exceeds 35 ft); M1502.4.3 (listed transition duct limited to 8 ft and not part of the duct length).
dryer-duct-length.freeAccess: The section requirements are cited by number. The code's fitting-equivalent TABLE is deliberately NOT reproduced: M1502.4.6.2 makes the manufacturer's values authoritative and the table a fallback, so both the ceiling and the per-fitting equivalents are user inputs here and no tabulated data is shipped.
dryer-duct-length.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
dryer-duct-length.editionNote: The 35 ft figure everyone quotes is the least useful number in the section, because fittings consume it. Developed length is the straight run plus the equivalent length of every elbow, and on a short interior run the fittings are routinely more than half the total - the tile reports that share explicitly so the imbalance is visible. The demonstration worth internalising is the fixture pair: the same 22 ft of duct with the same three 90s and two 45s comes to 42 ft on tight mitered elbows and 28 ft on wide smooth ones. Identical routing, identical fitting count, and compliance flips from 7 ft over to 7 ft to spare purely on elbow selection - which is almost always cheaper than rerouting duct or opening a wall, and is the first thing to price when a run comes up long. Following the code's own priority also settles the data question: M1502.4.6.2 states that the size and maximum length are determined by the DRYER MANUFACTURER'S installation instructions and that the code table applies only in the absence of manufacturer equivalent lengths. So the ceiling and the per-fitting values are inputs rather than shipped constants, the defaults are starting points to be replaced with the actual dryer's data, and no code table is reproduced. Two adjacent rules are flagged rather than silently ignored: over 35 ft of equivalent length M1502.4.7 requires a permanent label or tag within 6 ft of the duct connection, and the flexible TRANSITION duct is a separate listed assembly limited to 8 ft that is not part of this length at all - a distinction that trips people who measure from the appliance. Not checked: the 4 in nominal diameter and smooth-interior metal construction, support at 12 ft maximum intervals, joints made in the direction of airflow with no fastener penetrating more than 1/8 in, termination outdoors with a backdraft damper and no screen, the 3 ft separation from openings where the manufacturer is silent, protective shield plates, or booster fans. A screen; the dryer manufacturer's instructions, the adopted code, and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Developed length
assumptions.value: straight run plus every fitting's equivalent length

assumptions.name: Source of equivalents
assumptions.value: the dryer manufacturer first; the code table only in its absence - so both are INPUTS

assumptions.name: Elbow radius dominates
assumptions.value: a tight mitered 90 can cost more than three times a wide smooth one
assumptions.source: the spread within the code's own fitting table

assumptions.name: Label
assumptions.value: required over 35 ft of equivalent length, within 6 ft of the connection

assumptions.name: Transition duct
assumptions.value: listed, 8 ft maximum, and NOT counted in the duct length

assumptions.name: Not checked
assumptions.value: diameter, material, supports, joints, termination, damper, screens, shield plates, booster fans

pv-max-ambient-for-power.formula: T_cell = 25 + (target_power/P_stc - 1) x 100/gamma; max_ambient = T_cell - (NOCT - 20) x G/800. The inverse of P = P_stc x (1 + gamma/100 x (T_cell - 25)) and T_cell = T_amb + (NOCT - 20) x G/800.
pv-max-ambient-for-power.edition: The PV NOCT cell-temperature model and the datasheet power temperature coefficient, by name, solved for the ambient temperature.
pv-max-ambient-for-power.freeAccess: The NOCT model and temperature-coefficient derate are standard PV design relations (NREL / module datasheets). The module datasheet governs the coefficients.
pv-max-ambient-for-power.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
pv-max-ambient-for-power.editionNote: The highest ambient temperature a module still makes a target power, the inverse of the NOCT cell-temperature and power-derate model. Because the power coefficient gamma is negative (a hotter cell makes less power), this is a ceiling: above this ambient the module falls below the target. Cells run well above air temperature in sun (the NOCT rise), so the max ambient is well below the cell temperature. A target above the STC nameplate gives a max ambient below a 25 C cell (a cold-day-only output). This is the temperature derate only: it uses the entered NOCT and gamma and does not include soiling, wiring, inverter, or shading losses (see the performance-ratio tile). A design aid; the module datasheet governs.

assumptions.name: NOCT model
assumptions.value: max ambient = T_cell - (NOCT - 20) x G/800

assumptions.name: Power derate inverse
assumptions.value: T_cell = 25 + (target/P_stc - 1) x 100/gamma; gamma ~ -0.35%/C silicon

assumptions.name: Temperature only
assumptions.value: no irradiance scaling and no soiling/wiring/inverter/shading losses

settlement-limit-load.formula: d_sigma = sigma'0 (10^(Sc_ft (1 + e0) / (Cc H)) - 1), Sc_ft = Sc_in / 12; final_stress = sigma'0 + d_sigma.
settlement-limit-load.edition: The Terzaghi primary consolidation relation solved for the allowable load increment, the inverse of the settlement tile, as compiled in the Das and NAVFAC references, by name.
settlement-limit-load.freeAccess: The primary-consolidation relation is a public soil-mechanics result; NAVFAC DM-7 is public-domain and free online.
settlement-limit-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
settlement-limit-load.editionNote: The inverse of the primary-consolidation settlement: the maximum load-induced effective-stress increase d_sigma that holds a normally-consolidated clay's primary settlement to an allowable limit, from Sc = (Cc H/(1 + e0)) log10((sigma'0 + d_sigma)/sigma'0) solved for d_sigma = sigma'0 (10^(Sc(1 + e0)/(Cc H)) - 1). Because settlement grows with the log of the effective-stress RATIO, the allowable increment is a fraction of the existing stress and a tighter settlement limit allows disproportionately less load. It assumes a single normally-consolidated layer at one representative mid-layer stress (sublayer the profile for accuracy); it is not the immediate elastic settlement, secondary creep, or the time rate, and an OC clay needs the two-part Cr/Cc form. A design aid, not a substitute for the geotechnical engineer of record's report.

assumptions.name: Inverse relation
assumptions.value: d_sigma = sigma'0 (10^(Sc(1 + e0)/(Cc H)) - 1) at mid-layer

assumptions.name: Log stress ratio
assumptions.value: settlement grows with the log of the stress ratio, so a tighter limit allows disproportionately less load

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: single NC layer, one mid-layer stress, no time rate or secondary creep

slope-stability-seepage.formula: driving = gamma_sat H sin(beta) cos(beta); resisting = c' + (gamma_sat - 62.4) H cos^2(beta) tan(phi'); FS = resisting / driving. (c' = 0 gives FS = ((gamma_sat - 62.4)/gamma_sat) tan(phi')/tan(beta))
slope-stability-seepage.edition: The infinite-slope stability model with steady slope-parallel seepage on an effective-stress basis, as compiled in Das (Principles of Geotechnical Engineering) and the NAVFAC DM-7 slope-stability references, by name.
slope-stability-seepage.freeAccess: NAVFAC DM-7 is public-domain and free online; the seepage infinite-slope relations are public in the standard geotechnical texts; gamma_w = 62.4 pcf fresh water.
slope-stability-seepage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
slope-stability-seepage.editionNote: The infinite-slope factor of safety with steady seepage parallel to the slope and the water table at the surface, FS = (c' + (gamma_sat - gamma_w) H cos^2(beta) tan(phi')) / (gamma_sat H sin(beta) cos(beta)) with gamma_w = 62.4 pcf, and its cohesionless reduction FS = ((gamma_sat - gamma_w)/gamma_sat) tan(phi')/tan(beta), as compiled in the Das and NAVFAC slope-stability references. The pore pressure cuts the friction term to the buoyant weight while the driving weight stays saturated, so seepage roughly halves the cohesionless factor of safety versus the dry value (shown for contrast). Shallow translational slide, uniform infinite slope, drained effective-stress parameters, no seismic loading - not a circular Bishop/Spencer analysis; a working subdrain that relieves the seepage restores the dry value. A design/screening aid, not a substitute for a geotechnical engineer's stability analysis.

assumptions.name: Steady seepage at the surface
assumptions.value: the water table is at the slope surface with flow parallel to it (worst case); the friction term uses the buoyant weight gamma_sat - gamma_w while the driving term uses gamma_sat

assumptions.name: Cohesionless halving
assumptions.value: c' = 0 gives FS = ((gamma_sat - gamma_w)/gamma_sat) tan(phi')/tan(beta), about half the dry value for common soils

compressor-volumetric-efficiency.formula: compression_ratio = discharge_pressure_psia / suction_pressure_psia; volumetric_efficiency = 100 x (1 + C - C x (Pd/Ps)^(1/n)), C = clearance ratio (~0.03-0.06), n = polytropic re-expansion exponent (~1.11 R-22, 1.16 R-410A).
compressor-volumetric-efficiency.edition: Reciprocating compressor clearance volumetric efficiency (clearance-volume re-expansion; ASHRAE Refrigeration / Dossat Principles of Refrigeration), by name; the compressor's rated capacity at the operating condition governs.
compressor-volumetric-efficiency.freeAccess: The clearance re-expansion relation is public thermodynamics; the clearance ratio, the suction and discharge pressures, and the polytropic exponent come from the compressor and the operating condition.
compressor-volumetric-efficiency.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
compressor-volumetric-efficiency.editionNote: A reciprocating compressor cannot draw in a full cylinder of fresh suction vapor because a small CLEARANCE volume of gas is always left at the top of the stroke (over the piston and in the valve ports). At the end of the discharge stroke this clearance gas is at discharge pressure; as the piston starts down, it re-expands and refills part of the cylinder before the pressure drops enough to open the suction valve, so the intake of fresh low-pressure vapor is reduced. The clearance (theoretical) volumetric efficiency captures exactly this loss: VE = 1 + C - C x (Pd/Ps)^(1/n), where C is the clearance ratio (clearance volume divided by swept volume, typically 0.03 to 0.06), Pd/Ps is the absolute compression ratio (discharge over suction, both in absolute pressure), and n is the polytropic exponent of the re-expansion (about 1.11 for R-22, 1.16 for R-410A). A machine with a 0.045 clearance running a 300/70 = 4.3 absolute compression ratio on R-22 has a clearance VE of about 88%. The key behavior is that raising the head pressure -- from a dirty or undersized condenser, a hot day, or a high-lift application -- increases BOTH the compression ratio and the amount the trapped clearance gas re-expands, so the volumetric efficiency and therefore the pumped capacity fall together, which is why a compressor moves far less refrigerant at a high compression ratio. This equation gives only the CLEARANCE volumetric efficiency; the ACTUAL volumetric efficiency measured in the field is lower still, because the suction gas is heated (superheated) as it enters the warm cylinder and expands, because the suction and discharge valves and the piston rings leak, and because there is a pressure drop across the valves -- each of which subtracts several more percentage points. The actual pumped suction volume is the swept displacement times the volumetric efficiency. This is a reciprocating-compressor model; the manufacturer's published capacity at the actual operating condition governs.

assumptions.name: Clearance re-expansion
assumptions.value: VE = 1 + C - C x (Pd/Ps)^(1/n); C ~0.03-0.06, n ~1.11 R-22 / 1.16 R-410A; a higher compression ratio lowers VE

assumptions.name: Clearance VE only
assumptions.value: the actual VE is lower -- suction superheating, valve/ring leakage, and valve pressure drop each subtract more; actual pumped volume = displacement x VE; the rated capacity governs

fan-affinity-laws.formula: r = N2/N1; Q2 = Q1 r; SP2 = SP1 r^2; BHP2 = BHP1 r^3.
fan-affinity-laws.edition: The fan affinity (fan) laws for a speed change from AMCA / ASHRAE Handbook - Fundamentals, by name.
fan-affinity-laws.freeAccess: The affinity laws (flow proportional to speed, pressure to speed squared, power to speed cubed) are standard published fan-engineering relations.
fan-affinity-laws.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
fan-affinity-laws.editionNote: The fan affinity laws for a fixed fan at a changed speed: Q2 = Q1 (N2/N1), SP2 = SP1 (N2/N1)^2, and BHP2 = BHP1 (N2/N1)^3. The cube-law power relation is why a modest speed reduction saves large power (a 25% slowdown cuts brake horsepower about 58%), the basis of VFD energy savings. This assumes the same fan riding the same system curve; it does not capture motor/drive efficiency changes, belt losses, or a shifted system curve. A field aid; the manufacturer's fan curve and the equipment ratings govern.

assumptions.name: Affinity laws
assumptions.value: Q2 = Q1 r, SP2 = SP1 r^2, BHP2 = BHP1 r^3, r = N2/N1

assumptions.name: Same fan and system
assumptions.value: same fan on the same system curve; efficiency shifts not captured

assumptions.name: Design aid
assumptions.value: the manufacturer's fan curve and ratings govern

snow-guard-layout.formula: vector force (psf) = roof snow load x sin(roof angle); force per ft of eave = vector force x rafter (slope) length; guards per ft = force x safety factor / tested guard capacity; spacing = 12 / guards per ft.
snow-guard-layout.edition: Manufacturer snow-retention design method (roof snow x sine of the roof angle, times rafter length and tributary width), by name - not a code section.
snow-guard-layout.freeAccess: The method is published across independent snow-retention design references and manufacturer design guides.
snow-guard-layout.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
snow-guard-layout.editionNote: Only the sin(theta) component tries to slide, which is why a steep roof needs far more retention than a shallow one at the same snow load. THE HOLDING CAPACITY IS A MANUFACTURER TESTED VALUE AND IS NOT SHIPPED HERE: a clamp on a standing seam and a screw into a through-fastened panel are different numbers, and the panel or its fastening often fails before the guard does. The rafter length used is the SLOPE length, matching the manufacturer method; ASCE roof snow loads are defined on the horizontal projection, so this runs conservative by 1/cos(theta) - about 5% at 4:12 and 20% at 8:12 - and that is stated so a user reconciling against a code-based calculation knows why the numbers differ. Rows are assumed to share the load, which holds when they are spaced for comparable tributaries; concentrating rows near the eave changes the distribution. Above roughly 12:12 the standard method needs the manufacturer's steep-slope guidance. Retention keeps snow ON the roof, so the structure must be able to carry it - shedding was the previous load path. The manufacturer's tested data and the engineer of record govern.

assumptions.name: Vector force
assumptions.value: snow load x sin(roof angle); the cosine component is carried by the roof, not the guards

assumptions.name: Capacity is an input
assumptions.value: no holding capacity shipped; use tested data for the exact panel, seam, and attachment

assumptions.name: Slope length, stated
assumptions.value: rafter length used per the manufacturer method, conservative vs the horizontal projection by 1/cos(theta)

hydraulic-line-velocity.formula: V (ft/s) = [231 / (60 x 12)] x Q (gpm) / A (in^2) = 0.3208333 Q / A, A = pi/4 ID^2; minimum ID at a ceiling = sqrt(4 (K Q / Vmax) / pi); maximum flow = Vmax A / K.
hydraulic-line-velocity.edition: Continuity with derived unit conversion (231 cubic inches per gallon, 60 s/min, 12 in/ft) plus industry recommended-velocity bands, named as conventions rather than a standard.
hydraulic-line-velocity.freeAccess: The conversion is arithmetic; the recommended bands are published across hydraulic design references and component catalogs.
hydraulic-line-velocity.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hydraulic-line-velocity.editionNote: PUBLISHED BANDS DISAGREE and the tile says so instead of picking silently: one common set gives suction 2-4, return 4-13, and pressure 7-18 ft/s, while another gives suction 2-4, return 10-15, medium pressure 15-20, and high pressure 20-25. The defaults here are the more conservative set, the ceiling is an editable override, and only the suction band (2-4) is common to both - which is fitting, because suction is the strict one: too fast and the pump cavitates, which sounds like gravel and destroys the pump. Higher system pressures tolerate higher velocity, and continuous-duty circuits belong at the low end of whichever band you use. Enter the true hose ID, not the dash size or the OD. Velocity is one criterion: pressure drop, heat rejection, and the hose pressure rating are separate, and the hose manufacturer's data governs.

assumptions.name: Derived constant
assumptions.value: 0.3208333 is written in source as 231/(60 x 12) so it can be checked, not recalled

assumptions.name: Bands are conventions
assumptions.value: editable ceiling seeded by line type; both published sets named

assumptions.name: Velocity only
assumptions.value: pressure drop, heat rejection, and hose pressure rating are separate checks

seismic-approximate-period.formula: Ta = Ct hn^x. Table 12.8-2: steel MRF 0.028/0.8, concrete MRF 0.016/0.9, steel EBF/BRBF 0.03/0.75, other 0.02/0.75. Cu Ta upper limit from Table 12.8-1 (SD1).
seismic-approximate-period.edition: The ASCE 7 §12.8.2.1 approximate fundamental period Ta = Ct hn^x, with the Table 12.8-2 coefficients and the Table 12.8-1 Cu upper-limit factor, by name.
seismic-approximate-period.freeAccess: The approximate-period equation and the Ct/x and Cu tables are stated in ASCE 7 §12.8.2.1; the arithmetic is public. The structural height and SD1 are the user's own site/design inputs.
seismic-approximate-period.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
seismic-approximate-period.editionNote: The ASCE 7 §12.8.2.1 approximate fundamental period Ta = Ct hn^x (Eq. 12.8-7), the period the seismic-base-shear, vertical-distribution, and overturning tiles require but do not compute. hn is the structural height (base to roof, ft); Ct and x are the Table 12.8-2 coefficients by system (steel moment frames 0.028/0.8, concrete moment frames 0.016/0.9, steel eccentrically braced and buckling-restrained braced frames 0.03/0.75, all other structural systems 0.02/0.75). Ta is always permitted and is conservative (a shorter period lands higher on the design spectrum, giving a larger Cs); a period T from a rational (modal or Rayleigh) analysis may be used but not more than Cu Ta, the upper limit from Table 12.8-1 (Cu falls from 1.7 at SD1 <= 0.1 to 1.4 at SD1 >= 0.4). The moment-frame Ct/x apply only where the frame resists 100% of the seismic force and is not enclosed by more rigid components. A design aid, not a substitute for a licensed engineer's design.

assumptions.name: Approximate period
assumptions.value: Ta = Ct hn^x (hn base-to-roof structural height, ft)

assumptions.name: System coefficients
assumptions.value: steel MRF 0.028/0.8; concrete MRF 0.016/0.9; EBF/BRBF 0.03/0.75; other 0.02/0.75

assumptions.name: Cu Ta cap
assumptions.value: a computed T may be used up to Cu Ta; Cu 1.7 (SD1 <= 0.1) to 1.4 (SD1 >= 0.4)

scaffold-mudsill-bearing.formula: mudsill_area_ft2 = plank_width_in x plank_length_in / 144; bearing_psf = leg_load_lb / mudsill_area_ft2; required_area_ft2 = leg_load_lb / allowable_psf; required_length_in = required_area_ft2 x 144 / plank_width_in; pass = bearing_psf <= allowable_psf.
scaffold-mudsill-bearing.edition: Bearing-pressure identity by name (load / area vs allowable); OSHA 1926.451(c)(2) base-plate and mudsill foundation requirement.
scaffold-mudsill-bearing.freeAccess: OSHA 1926.451 is free at osha.gov; the load-over-area bearing check is public statics.
scaffold-mudsill-bearing.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
scaffold-mudsill-bearing.editionNote: The manufacturer's allowable base-plate load and the geotechnical allowable soil bearing govern - "looks solid" is not a number. OSHA 1926.451(c)(2) requires scaffold legs on base plates and mudsills on a sound, rigid foundation. Frost, voids, backfill, slopes, and adjacent excavations all cut soil capacity. A competent person verifies the setup; this is a first-check estimator, not the engineered design.

assumptions.name: Allowable soil bearing
assumptions.value: from the geotechnical report or a presumptive-load table; 2000 psf is the worked example's value only

assumptions.name: Mudsill board
assumptions.value: 9.25 in (a nominal 2x10) in the worked example; the actual plank width and length govern

propeller-track-balance.formula: track is compared against the manufacturer's limit; for balance the EFFECT vector is the trial reading minus the original, and the correction is the trial weight scaled by the ratio of the original to that effect, rotated so its effect opposes the original.
propeller-track-balance.edition: The track check against the manufacturer's limit and the single-plane trial-weight vector method. Readings are ENTERED from a calibrated analyser. It does not measure anything, validate the phase reference or tachometer pickup, address two-plane balancing, distinguish propeller imbalance from an engine or mount problem at the same frequency, or set the limits.
propeller-track-balance.freeAccess: One vector subtraction and one scaling.
propeller-track-balance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
propeller-track-balance.editionNote: Track and balance are DIFFERENT faults with different fixes and both produce vibration, which is why the track verdict comes before the balance arithmetic. Out of track means the blades sweep different planes, so each meets the air differently and the propeller generates a once-per-revolution AERODYNAMIC imbalance that no amount of weight corrects; out of balance is a mass distribution problem and that is what weight corrects. The effect vector is the DIFFERENCE between the two readings rather than the second reading, and a trial weight that produces no change in the vector has told you nothing -- which is reported rather than divided by. A static bench check finds a gross asymmetry and cannot find a dynamic couple.

assumptions.name: Track first
assumptions.value: a balance run on an out-of-track propeller chases a moving target

assumptions.name: Single plane
assumptions.value: a dynamic couple needs two-plane balancing

assumptions.name: Readings are entered
assumptions.value: the phase reference and tachometer pickup are not validated here

injection-clamp-tonnage.formula: clamp force = total projected area (parts plus runner, taken ALONG the mould opening direction) x cavity pressure, with a safety factor commonly 10 to 20%; the maximum cavity pressure a machine supports inverts it.
injection-clamp-tonnage.edition: Injection moulding clamp sizing as the trade states it, with cavity pressure ENTERED (typically 2 to 5 tons per in2) because it depends on wall thickness, flow length and material viscosity rather than on part size, and a mould flow analysis rather than a table is what a serious tool is sized on.
injection-clamp-tonnage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
injection-clamp-tonnage.editionNote: Projected area is got wrong in two ways and both show as flash. It is the area seen ALONG the mould opening direction rather than the part's surface area or its footprint, and it INCLUDES the runner, because a cold runner is pressurised plastic pushing the mould open exactly as the parts do. Cavity pressure is the term that moves most and the one this cannot supply: two parts of identical projected area can want machines a factor of two apart from geometry alone. Over-clamping is not free either -- it damages the parting line over time and ties up capacity -- so the answer is the right machine rather than the largest available.

assumptions.name: Cavity pressure is entered
assumptions.value: 2 to 5 tons per in2 typical, from geometry and material

assumptions.name: Projected area includes the runner
assumptions.value: a cold runner pressurises the mould

assumptions.name: Clamp only
assumptions.value: platen size, tie-bar spacing and stack height also decide fit

plenum-return-drop.formula: velocity at the restriction = return cfm / the clear area there; the area a target velocity requires = cfm / that target, and the width it implies at the same clear height; the measured room-to-plenum and plenum-to-shaft differences sum to the return path the fan actually carries.
plenum-return-drop.edition: The ceiling return plenum treated as a low-velocity duct whose restriction is at its pinch point, against the commonly cited 300 to 500 fpm plenum target. It computes velocity and the area a target requires; it does NOT compute the pressure drop, which depends on the shape of every obstruction, the approach conditions and the path length in ways a plenum's irregular geometry does not reduce to a coefficient. It does not model flow distribution across bays, fire and smoke dampers in the path, or the plenum's effect on return air temperature.
plenum-return-drop.freeAccess: One velocity and one area; measurement is the reliable method.
plenum-return-drop.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
plenum-return-drop.editionNote: A plenum is a duct whose cross-section is whatever the structure left over, and air does not distribute itself evenly through it -- it takes the easiest path, so a return that measures fine near the shaft can be starved at the far corner. The static consequence is what makes this a balancing issue: if the fan's external static assumed a negligible return and the plenum actually costs a measurable fraction of an inch, the fan delivers less than design at a HIGHER static than expected, which looks like a supply-side problem and is not. Measuring room to plenum and plenum to shaft is what localises it, and the split says whether the grille or the travel path is the culprit. The other consequence is pressure relationships: a restricted return makes the plenum more negative than the space and can undo the intended pressurization entirely.

assumptions.name: The pressure drop is not computed
assumptions.value: an irregular plenum geometry does not reduce to a coefficient

assumptions.name: One pinch point
assumptions.value: flow distribution across multiple bays is not modelled

assumptions.name: Dampers are not in the path model
assumptions.value: fire and smoke dampers add their own resistance

post-tension-elongation.formula: theoretical elongation = average force x length / (area x modulus), with force decaying along the tendon as exp(-(mu x alpha + K x)) and the average taken as the integral (1 - decay ratio) / exponent; the expected measured value is that less the anchor set, checked at an entered tolerance.
post-tension-elongation.edition: The post-tensioning elongation relation by name, with about 7% as the usual two-sided acceptance. Friction and wobble coefficients belong to the specific duct and tendon system and come from the post-tensioning supplier; strand area and modulus come from the mill certificate for the reel installed. The supplier's stressing calculations and elongation tables, ACI 318 and the PTI manuals, the mill certificates, and the engineer of record govern.
post-tension-elongation.freeAccess: One exponential and one division on properties from a mill certificate; no supplier elongation table is reproduced.
post-tension-elongation.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
post-tension-elongation.editionNote: Elongation measures the tendon's whole length responding to the force actually in it, which is why it catches what a gauge cannot: a gauge reads what the jack is pushing, and a tendon binding in a crushed duct shows up as elongation short of theoretical while the gauge reads exactly the specified pressure. The elongation follows the AVERAGE force along the length, not the jacking force, and using the jacking force directly overstates the expected stretch by a share of the 7% allowance that grows with friction and tendon length -- which makes a perfectly good tendon look like a failing one. The tolerance is two-sided: short means the force is not getting there, long means a wrong area, a wrong modulus, or slip. Both require investigation before grouting, because after grouting nothing can be corrected.

assumptions.name: Friction and wobble are entered
assumptions.value: they belong to the specific duct and tendon system

assumptions.name: Strand area and modulus from the mill certificate
assumptions.value: catalogue values where a certificate exists is a way tendons appear out of tolerance
assumptions.source: the mill certificate for the reel installed

assumptions.name: One prismatic member at a single average force
assumptions.value: no force profile, elastic shortening, relaxation, creep or sequence effects

plug-tray-cell-count.formula: usable per tray = cells x germination rate x (1 - cull rate); trays = plants required / usable per tray, rounded up.
plug-tray-cell-count.edition: The seed lot's own tested germination rate and the grower's observed cull at transplant govern; a published germination figure is a laboratory result under ideal conditions.
plug-tray-cell-count.freeAccess: Public arithmetic; germination is on the seed lot's own tag.
plug-tray-cell-count.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
plug-tray-cell-count.editionNote: The naive count -- the order divided by the cell count -- is short by the germination and cull losses together, and the shortage is found at TRANSPLANT, when a re-sow is weeks too late to ship with the crop.

assumptions.name: Germination
assumptions.value: the lot's tested rate, not the species average; field conditions are worse than the laboratory

assumptions.name: Bench area
assumptions.value: before aisles; the transplanted crop needs several times that on a different bench

sub-slab-suction-field.formula: area per point = pi x the confirmed radius squared; points on area = slab area / that; points by shape = the fewest points on a rectangular grid whose circles of the confirmed radius cover every corner of the slab (each cell's half-diagonal within the radius); the LARGER of the two governs.
sub-slab-suction-field.edition: A diagnostic communication test -- vacuum applied at a candidate point, a micromanometer read at test holes at increasing distances -- converted into a point count. The reach is MEASURED because nothing about it is calculable.
sub-slab-suction-field.freeAccess: Circle area and a spacing count on entered test readings.
sub-slab-suction-field.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sub-slab-suction-field.editionNote: SHAPE GOVERNS MORE OFTEN THAN AREA, and a coverage figure alone hides it. The 1,600 sq ft slab in the source case needs 1 point on area -- a 25 ft radius covers 1,963 sq ft -- but 2 to cover an 80 by 20 ft run, and even a compact 40 by 40 ft slab of identical area needs 2, because one 25 ft circle at its center leaves the corners (28.3 ft out) uncovered. On a tight sub-slab with a 6 ft field the 80 by 20 slab needs 26, not the 15 its area alone suggests. Both checks are made here and the larger is reported, because designing on coverage alone under-counts every corridor-shaped building. THE SUB-SLAB MATERIAL DECIDES EVERYTHING and varies between ends of one house: clean gravel carries a field twenty-five or thirty feet, a slab on compacted fines gives a few. A BIGGER FAN DOES NOT FIX POOR COMMUNICATION -- it pulls harder on the same small area. And the test costs an hour BEFORE installation; the same finding after a failed post-mitigation measurement costs a second mobilisation and a second penetration.

assumptions.name: The confirmed radius is the design input
assumptions.value: not the distance at which vacuum was absent

assumptions.name: Circular field assumed
assumptions.value: footings and slab joints compartmentalise it in reality

assumptions.name: Grid coverage
assumptions.value: points on a rectangular grid, each cell within one radius of its point at the corners (a 1.41-radius square cell), so the whole slab is inside some field -- not circles spaced two radii apart, which leaves the gaps between them
